questions.stem: The Viking homelands were in which present-day countries?
options: Finland, Estonia and Latvia
Norway, Sweden and Denmark
Germany, Poland and the Netherlands
Ireland, Scotland and Wales
questions.explanation: The Vikings came from Scandinavia — today's Norway, Sweden and Denmark — where long coastlines, fjords and limited farmland pushed people to the sea. Ireland and Scotland were places Vikings raided and settled, not their homelands.

questions.stem: The Viking raid on the monastery of Lindisfarne in 793 is often taken as:
options: the founding of the Viking town of Dublin
the start of the Viking Age raids on Britain
the end of the Viking Age in Britain and Ireland
the first Viking landing in North America
questions.explanation: The attack on Lindisfarne, an island monastery off north-east England, shocked Christian Europe and is traditionally seen as the beginning of the Viking Age. The Viking Age is usually said to end around 1066, almost three centuries later.

questions.stem: Why do historians think early written accounts may exaggerate Viking violence?
options: Most were based on archaeology that has since been disproved
Most were written by Arab traders who had never met any Vikings
Most were written by monks, whose monasteries were the targets of raids
Most were written by Vikings boasting about their own victories and treasure
questions.explanation: Monks were among the few people who could write, and monasteries — full of treasure and poorly defended — were frequent targets, so their accounts were written by terrified victims. The Vikings themselves left few written records apart from short runestone inscriptions.

questions.stem: What were the three main classes in Viking society?
options: Jarls, karls and thralls
Lords, knights and serfs
Patricians, plebeians and slaves
Doges, guildsmen and labourers
questions.explanation: Jarls were wealthy chieftains, karls were free farmers, craftspeople and traders, and thralls were enslaved people. Lords, knights and serfs describe the feudal society of medieval Christian Europe.

questions.stem: In Viking society, who were thralls?
options: Free farmers who owned their own land
Priests who led sacrifices to Odin and Thor
Enslaved people, often captured in raids
Wealthy chieftains who led war bands
questions.explanation: Thralls were enslaved people with almost no rights; many were captured in raids on Britain, Ireland and eastern Europe and some were sold in slave markets. Free farmers were karls, the largest group in Viking society.

questions.stem: What was the Thing in Viking society?
options: An assembly of free men that made laws and settled disputes
A sacred temple where Odin and Thor were worshipped
The king's personal bodyguard of the best warriors
A wooden fort that guarded the entrance to an important trading town
questions.explanation: At the Thing, free men met to make laws, settle disputes and judge cases; Iceland's Althing, founded in 930, is often called one of the world's oldest parliaments. Worship of the gods took place at separate sacred sites and feasts.

questions.stem: Compared with many other European women of the time, Viking women:
options: were all trained to fight as shield-maidens
could vote for kings at the Thing assembly
could not inherit anything from their families
could own property and could seek a divorce
questions.explanation: Viking women ran farms and households, held the keys to the family's stores, could own property and could seek a divorce. Women could not speak or vote at the Thing, and while stories of shield-maidens exist, there is no evidence that women were generally trained as warriors.

questions.stem: Which Viking god carried a hammer and was linked with thunder?
options: Thor
Odin
Freyja
Loki
questions.explanation: Thor, the thunder god, carried the hammer Mjölnir, and many Vikings wore small hammer pendants for protection. Odin was the chief god, linked with wisdom, poetry and war.

questions.stem: In Viking belief, what was Valhalla?
options: The rainbow bridge linking the world of humans and Asgard
The underworld ruled by Hel for those who died of illness
The hall of Odin, where warriors who died in battle feasted
The great ash tree said to hold up the nine worlds
questions.explanation: Valhalla was Odin's great hall, where chosen warriors killed in battle feasted while waiting to fight at Ragnarök, the end of the world. The great ash tree holding the worlds is Yggdrasil, and the rainbow bridge is Bifröst.

questions.stem: Which feature of the Viking longship made surprise raids far inland possible?
options: Three tall masts carrying many square and triangular sails
An iron-plated hull that protected the crew from arrows
A shallow hull that let it sail up rivers and land on beaches
A deep, heavy hull that needed a harbour to unload safely
questions.explanation: Longships needed very little water, so they could be rowed up rivers such as the Seine and run straight onto a beach, letting raiders strike and escape before defenders gathered. They had one mast with a single square sail, plus oars.

questions.stem: Viking ships were clinker-built. What does this mean?
options: The planks were laid smoothly edge to edge over a strong inner frame
The hull was hollowed out from a single large tree trunk
The hull was made of animal skins stretched over a frame
The planks of the hull overlapped and were riveted together
questions.explanation: In clinker building, each hull plank overlaps the one below and is fastened with iron rivets, making a light, flexible and strong hull. Planks laid edge to edge over a frame is carvel building, a different method used later for larger ships.

questions.stem: Jorvik was the Viking name for which modern city in England?
options: London
Dover
Bristol
York
questions.explanation: Viking settlers captured York in 866 and made Jorvik a busy trading town; excavations at Coppergate uncovered houses, workshops and thousands of everyday objects. Dublin, in Ireland, was another major Viking town.

questions.stem: What was the Danelaw?
options: The peace treaty that sent all the Vikings home from England
The part of England where Danish Vikings ruled and their laws applied
The payments English kings made to the Vikings to stop them raiding again
The law-making assembly that met each summer in Denmark
questions.explanation: After fighting Alfred the Great, the Vikings controlled much of northern and eastern England, where Danish law and customs applied — the Danelaw. Payments to buy off raiders are called Danegeld, a different term that is easily confused with it.

questions.stem: How did Normandy, in northern France, come to be named?
options: Charlemagne named it after a victory over the Northmen
Land there was granted to the 'Northmen' led by Rollo in 911
It was settled by Normans who crossed from England after 1066
A Norwegian king conquered all of France and named it after himself
questions.explanation: In 911 the West Frankish king Charles the Simple granted land around Rouen to the Viking leader Rollo, hoping he would defend it against other raiders; the 'Northmen' became the Normans. The Normans conquered England in 1066 from Normandy, not the other way round.

questions.stem: Archaeologists have found a Viking settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows. Where is it?
options: Iceland
Northern Ireland
Newfoundland, Canada
Greenland
questions.explanation: L'Anse aux Meadows, on the northern tip of Newfoundland, is the only confirmed Viking site in North America. Greenland had Viking farms too — settled by Erik the Red's followers from about 985 — and Leif Erikson sailed west from there.

questions.stem: Why is the site at L'Anse aux Meadows historically significant?
options: It shows the Vikings reached North America before they settled Iceland
It proves the Vikings traded regularly with the Aztecs of Mexico
It shows Europeans reached the Americas about 500 years before Columbus
It proves Vikings built permanent towns across most of North America
questions.explanation: Tree-ring dating shows Vikings were cutting wood at the site in 1021 CE, nearly five centuries before Columbus arrived in 1492. The settlement was small and short-lived, so it does not show permanent Viking towns across the continent.

questions.stem: Scandinavians who travelled east along the rivers of Russia reached Constantinople, where some became bodyguards of the Byzantine emperor. What was this force called?
options: The Knights Templar
The Janissaries
The Praetorian Guard
The Varangian Guard
questions.explanation: The Varangian Guard was the Byzantine emperor's elite bodyguard, made up largely of Scandinavians and later Anglo-Saxons. The Praetorian Guard protected the emperors of ancient Rome, centuries earlier.

questions.stem: In 1066 the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada was killed at the Battle of Stamford Bridge. Who defeated him?
options: King Alfred the Great of Wessex
King Cnut, ruler of Denmark and England
King Harold Godwinson of England
Duke William of Normandy
questions.explanation: Harold Godwinson defeated Hardrada near York in September 1066, then marched south and was killed by William of Normandy at Hastings a few weeks later. Alfred the Great died in 899, so he could not have fought in 1066.

questions.stem: Which best explains why the Viking Age came to an end around 1066?
options: The Black Death wiped out most of the Scandinavian people in the eleventh century
Iron ran out in Scandinavia, so no more weapons could be made
Every Viking settlement in Britain and France was abandoned by 1000
Christian, centralised kingdoms replaced independent raiding chieftains
questions.explanation: As Denmark, Norway and Sweden became Christian kingdoms under strong kings, raiding gave way to trade, alliances and ordinary warfare between states, and the settlers merged into local populations. The Black Death struck in the 1340s, nearly three hundred years after the Viking Age ended.

questions.stem: The Icelandic sagas were written down in the 1200s and 1300s. Why must historians use them carefully as evidence of the Viking Age?
options: They were written by English monks who wanted to make the Vikings look evil
They were carved in runes that no one has been able to read for centuries
They were tax records kept by Viking kings and leave out daily life entirely
They were recorded around two centuries after many of the events they describe
questions.explanation: The sagas were written by Christian Icelanders long after the events, drawing on stories passed down orally, so they mix history with legend and later values. They are still valuable, especially when archaeology, such as the finds at L'Anse aux Meadows, confirms parts of them.

questions.stem: What made the Viking expansion overseas possible?
options: A peace treaty that let Viking ships sail freely into every European port
Skilled shipbuilding and navigation, combined with a search for land and wealth
A single Viking emperor who ordered every Scandinavian family to conquer new lands
Maps and compasses bought from the Chinese along the Silk Roads
questions.explanation: Fast, seaworthy ships and navigation by sun, stars, coastlines and birds let Vikings cross open seas, while a shortage of good farmland and the lure of trade and plunder gave them reasons to go. Scandinavia was divided among many chieftains and kings, so no single ruler directed the expansion.
